title: Amiga 68000 Assembly School
subtitle: Learn 68000 assembly, Amiga custom chips, and system-friendly programs by running real code.

lessons.title: What is assembly, and why 68000?
lessons.subtitle: Build the mental model
lessons.goal: Understand how assembly maps directly to CPU actions.
theory: In Swift, the compiler translates your intent into machine instructions. In assembly, you write that translation yourself.
The Motorola 68000 is a friendly first CPU because its instructions are regular and readable.
lessons.analogy: Swift asks for array.sort(). Assembly writes the comparisons, swaps, and storage choices by hand.
lessons.keyIdea: Computation happens in registers first. Memory is where data waits.
lessons.starterCode:
; The smallest useful program
    moveq #0,d0
    rts

quiz.question: Where does computation happen first on the 68000?
quiz.feedback: Correct. The CPU mostly computes in registers, then stores results back to memory or hardware.

lessons.title: The register file
lessons.subtitle: D0-D7 and A0-A7
lessons.goal: Use data registers for values and address registers for pointers.
theory: The 68000 gives you eight data registers, D0 through D7, and eight address registers, A0 through A7.
A7 is also the stack pointer, so it has a special role in every subroutine call.
lessons.analogy: A Swift variable such as total becomes a deliberate register choice such as D0.
lessons.keyIdea: MOVE source,destination is the basic assembly rhythm; destination is on the right.
lessons.starterCode:
; Put the result in D0
    moveq #10,d0
    moveq #7,d1
    add.l d1,d0
    subq.l #2,d0
    rts

quiz.question: Which register is normally the stack pointer?
quiz.feedback: Correct. A7 is the stack pointer, also written as SP.

lessons.title: MOVE: your first instruction
lessons.subtitle: Constants, registers, and sizes
lessons.goal: Make D0 contain 42 by moving and adding values.
theory: MOVE copies data. It does not destroy the source.
MOVEQ is a compact form for loading small immediate values into data registers.
Instruction suffixes matter: .b is a byte, .w is a word, and .l is a longword.
lessons.analogy: Swift hides integer width most of the time. Assembly makes the width visible.
lessons.keyIdea: Always know which operand is the destination because that is the value that changes.
lessons.starterCode:
; Predict D0, then run it
    moveq #5,d0
    move.l d0,d1
    addq.l #3,d1
    move.l d1,d0
    rts

quiz.question: After move.l d0,d1, what happens to D0?
quiz.feedback: Exactly. MOVE copies the source value; it does not consume it.

lessons.title: Arithmetic: ADD, SUB, MULS
lessons.subtitle: Do math one instruction at a time
lessons.goal: Combine arithmetic instructions and inspect the result in D0.
theory: ADD and SUB modify the destination operand.
MULS multiplies signed values and produces a 32-bit result in a data register.
lessons.analogy: score += 300 becomes an ADD instruction after score has been loaded into D0.
lessons.keyIdea: A register is both your workspace and your result, so track every mutation.
lessons.starterCode:
; Make D0 equal 42
    moveq #6,d0
    moveq #7,d1
    muls d1,d0
    rts

quiz.question: Which side changes in add.l d1,d0?
quiz.feedback: Right. D0 receives D0 + D1 because it is the destination.

lessons.title: Branching and loops
lessons.subtitle: BEQ, BNE, DBRA
lessons.goal: Build loop behavior from labels, flags, and branches.
theory: Assembly has no if or while keyword. You make control flow with labels and branches.
CMP sets CPU flags, and conditional branches read those flags.
DBRA decrements a data register and branches while it has not reached -1.
lessons.analogy: A Swift loop has a hidden test and jump. Assembly makes both explicit.
lessons.keyIdea: Branches are how code stops being a straight line.
lessons.starterCode:
; Add 5 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1
    moveq #0,d0
    moveq #5,d1
loop:
    add.w d1,d0
    subq.w #1,d1
    bne loop
    rts

quiz.question: What makes bne loop jump?
options: The previous result was not zero
quiz.feedback: Yes. BNE branches when the zero flag is clear.

lessons.title: Memory and addressing
lessons.subtitle: Labels, pointers, and offsets
lessons.goal: Recognize labels as addresses and use address registers as pointers.
theory: A label is a readable name for an address.
LEA loads the address of a label, not the bytes stored there.
Offset addressing such as 2(a0) means memory at A0 plus 2.
lessons.analogy: A Swift array access hides address math. In 68k, the address math is visible in the operand.
lessons.keyIdea: Memory only becomes meaningful when you know its layout.
lessons.starterCode:
; A tiny struct-like layout
    moveq #0,d0
    move.w #1200,d0
    add.w #300,d0
    rts

quiz.question: What does lea player,a0 load?
quiz.feedback: Correct. LEA means load effective address.

lessons.title: Subroutines: JSR and RTS
lessons.subtitle: Calls, returns, and the stack
lessons.goal: Call a helper routine and return with the result in D0.
theory: BSR and JSR call subroutines. RTS returns to the saved address.
The return address is saved on the stack, which uses A7.
lessons.analogy: A Swift function call has a calling convention too. Assembly makes that contract visible.
lessons.keyIdea: Every routine should document its inputs, outputs, and preserved registers.
lessons.starterCode:
; Double D0 with a helper
    moveq #21,d0
    bsr double_d0
    rts

double_d0:
    add.l d0,d0
    rts

quiz.question: What instruction returns from a 68k subroutine?
quiz.feedback: Right. RTS restores the saved return address and continues after the call.

lessons.title: Your first Amiga program
lessons.subtitle: Write to hardware
lessons.goal: Write a color value directly to the Amiga COLOR00 register.
theory: Amiga custom chips are mapped into memory, so writing to a hardware address changes hardware state.
$DFF180 is COLOR00, the background color register.
lessons.analogy: Swift calls an API. Classic Amiga code can write directly to a hardware register.
lessons.keyIdea: The CPU, Copper, Blitter, Paula, and Agnus form the Amiga personality.

quiz.question: What is special about $DFF180?
options: It is the background color register
quiz.feedback: Yes. COLOR00 lives at $DFF180, so writing a color word changes the background color.

lessons.title: Interrupts and the vertical blank
lessons.subtitle: Let the hardware call your code
lessons.goal: Understand how interrupt requests, masks, and return-from-interrupt work together.
theory: An interrupt lets hardware pause normal code and request a short service routine.
The Amiga interrupt registers separate requests from enables, so software can acknowledge an event and decide which events are allowed through.
A level-3 handler returns with RTE, which restores the saved status register as well as the program counter.
lessons.analogy: A Swift callback runs when an event arrives. An interrupt is the CPU-level version, with the processor saving enough state to resume later.
lessons.keyIdea: A request is not the same thing as an enabled interrupt; both sides of the handshake matter.
lessons.starterCode:
; Enable the vertical blank interrupt bit
            move.w     #$c020,$dff09a
            move.w     #$0020,$dff09c
            rte

quiz.question: Which instruction returns from an interrupt handler?
quiz.feedback: Correct. RTE restores the interrupted status and continues the suspended program.

lessons.title: The Copper coprocessor
lessons.subtitle: Change hardware during the display beam
lessons.goal: Build a Copper list that changes a color register at a chosen raster position.
theory: The Copper is a tiny display-synchronized coprocessor that executes MOVE, WAIT, and SKIP instructions.
A Copper list lives in chip memory and can update custom-chip registers without spending CPU instructions on every scanline.
The list ends with a WAIT that never becomes true, commonly written as $ffff,$fffe.
lessons.analogy: Instead of scheduling every frame update from Swift, you hand the video hardware a tiny timeline to replay alongside the beam.
lessons.keyIdea: The Copper turns beam position into a programmable event source.
lessons.starterCode:
; Install a tiny Copper list
            SECTION    Code,CODE,CHIP
            lea        $dff000,a5
            lea        CopperList(pc),a0
            move.l     a0,$80(a5)
            move.w     #$0000,$88(a5)
            move.w     #$8280,$96(a5)
            rts
CopperList:
            dc.w       $0180,$0000
            dc.w       $0180,$0f00
            dc.w       $ffff,$fffe

quiz.question: What does a Copper WAIT synchronize with?
quiz.feedback: Exactly. A WAIT pauses the Copper until the programmed beam position is reached.

lessons.title: Bitplanes and playfields
lessons.subtitle: How Amiga pixels become colors
lessons.goal: Explain planar graphics and connect a bitplane pointer to the display hardware.
theory: Amiga OCS graphics are planar: each bitplane contributes one bit to the final color index at each pixel.
One bitplane gives two colors, two give four, and so on. The playfield hardware combines the planes with the color registers.
The bitplane pointers, display window, data fetch, and BPLCON0 must agree about where and how the screen is drawn.
lessons.analogy: A chunky pixel stores one color value. A planar pixel is more like several Swift Bool arrays whose bits are combined into an index.
lessons.keyIdea: The screen is not a bitmap of color values; it is a stack of synchronized one-bit images.
lessons.starterCode:
; Point one bitplane at chip memory and enable it
            SECTION    Code,CODE,CHIP
            lea        $dff000,a5
            lea        Plane0(pc),a0
            move.l     a0,$e0(a5)
            move.w     #$1200,$100(a5)
            move.w     #$8300,$96(a5)
            rts
Plane0:
            dc.w       %1111000011110000,%0000111100001111
            dc.w       %1111111111111111,%0000000000000000

quiz.question: How many color choices can two enabled bitplanes represent?
quiz.feedback: Right. Two binary planes combine into four possible color indexes.

lessons.title: Hardware sprites
lessons.subtitle: Objects the display draws for you
lessons.goal: Recognize the sprite data structure and install a hardware sprite pointer.
theory: A hardware sprite is a separate display object with position/control words followed by two bitplanes of sprite data.
The sprite pointer registers tell the custom chips where the structure lives in chip memory.
A terminating zero control pair ends the sprite, and the sprite DMA channel must be enabled before it appears.
lessons.analogy: A sprite is a small hardware-managed view layer: you provide its data and coordinates, and the display system composites it over the playfield.
lessons.keyIdea: Hardware sprites do not need to be copied into the playfield every frame.

quiz.question: Where does a hardware sprite's image data live?
quiz.feedback: Correct. The sprite pointer targets a chip-memory structure containing position, control, and image words.

lessons.title: The Blitter
lessons.subtitle: Copy, combine, fill, and draw
lessons.goal: Set up an A-to-D Blitter copy and understand its minterm and size controls.
theory: The Blitter moves and combines chip-memory words using up to three sources, A, B, and C, and one destination, D.
BLTCON0's minterm describes the Boolean function while its USE bits select active channels.
Pointers, masks, modulos, and BLTSIZE define the exact rectangle. The CPU can continue other work while the Blitter runs.
lessons.analogy: A Blitter is a dedicated memory kernel: instead of looping over every pixel in Swift, you configure the operation and let the custom chip stream the block.
lessons.keyIdea: The Blitter is a programmable Boolean engine, not just a fast memcpy.
lessons.starterCode:
; Copy a one-word-wide block from A to D
            SECTION    Code,CODE,CHIP
            lea        $dff000,a5
            lea        Source(pc),a0
            lea        Destination(pc),a1
            move.l     a0,$50(a5)
            move.l     a1,$54(a5)
            move.w     #$09f0,$40(a5)
            move.w     #$ffff,$44(a5)
            move.w     #$ffff,$46(a5)
            move.w     #$4041,$58(a5)
            rts
Source:
            ds.w       64
Destination:
            ds.w       64

quiz.question: What does the Blitter minterm control?
options: The Boolean combination of A, B, and C
quiz.feedback: Yes. The minterm is the eight-entry truth-table function applied to the enabled source channels.

lessons.title: Paula audio DMA
lessons.subtitle: Play a waveform without a CPU loop
lessons.goal: Configure an audio channel pointer, length, period, volume, and DMA enable.
theory: Paula's audio channels stream signed waveform bytes from chip memory using DMA.
The channel needs a data pointer, a word length, a period that sets the sample rate, and a volume from 0 through 64.
Audio DMA is enabled through DMACON, alongside the global DMA enable bit.
lessons.analogy: The CPU does not call a play-sample function for every byte. It submits a buffer and playback parameters to a hardware queue.
lessons.keyIdea: DMA turns a memory buffer into a time-based hardware stream.
lessons.starterCode:
; Start a short tone on audio channel 0
            SECTION    Code,CODE,CHIP
            lea        $dff000,a5
            lea        Wave(pc),a0
            move.l     a0,$a0(a5)
            move.w     #4,$a4(a5)
            move.w     #$0070,$a6(a5)
            move.w     #$0040,$a8(a5)
            move.w     #$8201,$96(a5)
            rts
Wave:
            dc.b       $00,$40,$7f,$40,$00,$c0,$81,$c0

quiz.question: Which value controls the audio channel's sample playback rate?
quiz.feedback: Correct. AUDxPER sets the period between samples; a smaller period means a higher playback rate.

lessons.title: System-friendly Amiga programming
lessons.subtitle: Use Exec and graphics.library
lessons.goal: Understand library bases, negative offsets, and why programs should cooperate with the Amiga OS.
theory: AmigaOS exposes services through library bases and jump tables rather than a modern object method call.
ExecBase is available at address 4, and library calls use negative offsets from the library base in A6.
System-friendly code saves registers, opens libraries, uses OS APIs, and restores the display before returning.
lessons.analogy: Direct hardware access is like reaching behind a Swift framework's public API. Library calls are the supported interface that lets other tasks and the OS keep working.
lessons.keyIdea: Takeover demos can own the machine; applications should cooperate with the machine.
lessons.starterCode:
; Open graphics.library and wait for a frame
            SECTION    Code,CODE
            XDEF       _Start
_Start:
            move.l     $4.w,a6
            lea        GraphicsName(pc),a1
            moveq      #0,d0
            jsr        -408(a6)
            move.l     d0,a6
            beq.s      .done
            jsr        -270(a6)
.done:
            rts
GraphicsName:
            dc.b       'graphics.library',0
            even

quiz.question: Where does an Amiga program find ExecBase?
quiz.feedback: Right. The longword at address 4 points to the ExecBase library structure.

lessons.title: Build a complete Amiga executable
lessons.subtitle: From source file to runnable Hunk
lessons.goal: Connect assembly sections, exported symbols, startup code, linking, and a clean return path.
theory: An executable is more than instructions: it has sections, symbols, relocation information, and an entry point understood by the linker and loader.
A typical Amiga build assembles source into an object or Hunk file, links it with startup code and libraries, then produces an executable that the OS can load.
A real program documents its calling contract, preserves registers it does not own, and returns a meaningful result or exits through the appropriate startup layer.
lessons.analogy: Swift source becomes an app through compilation and linking. The Amiga workflow exposes those same stages, so you can see where symbols and libraries enter the final program.
lessons.keyIdea: Assembly is one stage of a program’s build pipeline, not the whole executable format.
lessons.starterCode:
; A linkable entry point with a preserved register set
            SECTION    Code,CODE
            XDEF       _main
_main:
            MOVEM.L    D2-D7/A2-A6,-(SP)
            MOVEQ      #0,D0
            MOVEM.L    (SP)+,D2-D7/A2-A6
            RTS

quiz.question: What does the linker add that a single assembly source file does not provide by itself?
quiz.feedback: Exactly. The linker resolves symbols and lays sections out into a loadable program.
